subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Active transport differs from facilitated diffusion because active transport:
options: moves substances down a concentration gradient
only moves water molecules
requires ATP to move substances against their concentration gradient via carrier proteins
does not use membrane proteins
questions.explain: Active transport uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to pump substances against their gradient through carrier proteins.

questions.q: Enzymes increase the rate of reaction by:
options: raising the temperature of the substrate
lowering the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway
increasing the activation energy of the reaction
being permanently changed by the reaction
questions.explain: Enzymes lower the activation energy required, allowing more substrate molecules to react at a given temperature.

questions.q: ATP is described as the universal energy currency because:
options: it stores energy long-term like glycogen
hydrolysis of its terminal phosphate releases a manageable quantity of energy for cellular reactions
its hydrolysis releases a large, fixed amount of energy in a single immediate step
it cannot be regenerated once hydrolysed
questions.explain: ATP releases a small, usable amount of energy when its terminal phosphate bond is hydrolysed to ADP and Pi, and is rapidly resynthesised.

questions.q: The Golgi apparatus is mainly responsible for:
options: modifying, packaging and sorting proteins into vesicles for secretion
producing ATP
replicating DNA
synthesising ribosomal RNA
questions.explain: The Golgi modifies proteins (e.g. adding carbohydrate), packages them into vesicles and labels them for their destination.

questions.q: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction typically decrease over time when measured as product formed?
options: The enzyme is denatured by the product
The temperature continually rises
The activation energy increases over time
Substrate concentration falls as it is converted to product, reducing collision frequency
questions.explain: As substrate is depleted, fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, so the rate declines until substrate runs out.

questions.q: On a rate-against-substrate-concentration graph, increasing the concentration of a COMPETITIVE inhibitor would:
options: have no effect on the curve
prevent Vmax ever being reached even at infinite substrate
increase the substrate concentration needed to reach the same rate, but Vmax is still attainable
lower the Vmax that can be reached
questions.explain: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by sufficient substrate, so Vmax is unchanged but more substrate is needed to approach it.

questions.q: Out of every six molecules of triose phosphate (TP) made in the Calvin cycle, how many are used to regenerate RuBP?
options: Six
Two
Five
Three
questions.explain: Five of every six TP molecules are recycled to regenerate RuBP, leaving one to contribute to carbohydrate.

questions.q: In which cellular location does glycolysis occur, and which type of phosphorylation produces its ATP?
options: Mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation
Inner mitochondrial membrane; chemiosmosis
Cytoplasm; substrate-level phosphorylation
Thylakoid membrane; photophosphorylation
questions.explain: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and generates ATP directly by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.q: Which factor would increase the permeability of a cell membrane?
options: Increasing cholesterol content
A decrease in temperature, increasing phospholipid order
Removal of all membrane proteins
An increase in temperature, increasing phospholipid movement and creating gaps
questions.explain: Higher temperatures increase phospholipid kinetic energy and fluidity, and can denature membrane proteins, increasing permeability.

questions.q: The sodium-potassium pump in co-transport maintains a low intracellular Na+ concentration by:
options: breaking down the cell membrane
actively pumping 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in using ATP
allowing Na+ to diffuse passively out
pumping glucose out of the cell
questions.explain: The Na+/K+ ATPase actively exports 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+ per ATP, creating the Na+ gradient that powers glucose co-transport.

questions.q: Which feature of the chloroplast increases the surface area available for the light-dependent reactions?
options: The double outer envelope
The fluid-filled stroma
The stacked thylakoid membranes forming grana
The presence of starch grains
questions.explain: Thylakoids stacked into grana give a large membrane surface area for photosystems and electron carriers.

questions.q: In mammalian muscle during anaerobic respiration, what is the key role of reducing pyruvate to lactate?
options: To regenerate NAD so glycolysis can continue
To synthesise acetyl CoA for the Krebs cycle
To generate additional ATP directly
To produce carbon dioxide for gas exchange
questions.explain: Reducing pyruvate oxidises reduced NAD back to NAD, allowing glycolysis and its ATP yield to continue without oxygen.
